descriptionChirho: Intransitive sense: to stand in a place, be in a standing position, or rise to one's feet — the core physical-positional meaning of the intransitive 2nd aorist (ἔστην), perfect (ἕστηκα), and pluperfect stems. All voices and tenses share the common meaning of bodily upright position. Cross-linguistic evidence: Arabic وَاقِف / يَقِف (standing, positional), Korean 서다 / 서 있다 (to stand / be standing), Swahili -simama (stand), Hindi खड़ा होना (to stand), Spanish 'de pie / estar de pie'.

Figurative-metaphorical intransitive sense: to stand firm, remain steadfast, endure, or persist — used of moral, spiritual, or institutional endurance rather than physical position. Distinguished by Arabic يَثْبُتُ / ثابِت (to be firm, endure) rather than positional وَاقِف; Spanish 'estar firme / permanecer' (stand firm / remain); Korean 서다 in contexts of withstanding; Hindi टिकना (to endure). Includes future and subjunctive forms referring to ability to withstand (e.g., 'who can stand?').

Transitive causative sense: to set, place, or cause someone/something to stand — the core meaning of the active 1st aorist (ἔστησα) and present active in transitive use. Distinguished by Arabic أَقَامَ / أَوْقَفَ (causative: to set up, place upright), Korean 세우다 (to erect, set up), Swahili -simamisha (causative of -simama), Hindi खड़ा करना (to cause to stand), Spanish 'poner / presentar'. Includes passive forms where the subject is caused to stand by another agent (Arabic سَتَقِفُونَ, Hindi खड़े किए जाओगे, Spanish 'seréis puestos').

Intransitive cessative sense: to stop, halt, stand still, or cease moving — an ingressive-to-resultative shift from motion to stasis. Distinguished by Korean 멈추다 / 멈춰 서다 (to stop, halt) rather than plain 서다; Spanish 'detenerse / cesar' (to stop / cease); Hindi रुकना / ठहरना (to stop); Arabic وَقَفَ in cessative contexts. Applies to persons halting on a journey and to natural phenomena ceasing (e.g., a flow of blood stopping).

Abstract causative sense: to establish, confirm, uphold, or appoint — used of laws, covenants, institutions, or divine purposes. Distinguished by Arabic يُثَبِّتُ / عَيَّنَ (to confirm, establish, appoint) and passive يُثَبَّتُ; Korean 세우다 in institutional contexts; Swahili -thibitisha (to confirm, establish); Hindi स्थापित करना (to establish); Spanish 'establecer'. Includes the passive 'be established' (Arabic تَثْبُتَ, Swahili lithibitishwe).

Specialized commercial sense: to weigh out or set (a price/payment) — used in transactional contexts involving money or wages. Distinguished uniquely by Arabic وَزَنُوا (they weighed) rather than أَقَامُوا; Spanish 'pesaron' (they weighed); Hindi ठहराए (they fixed/settled). This reflects the ancient practice of weighing silver as payment.
